newsitem.title: UK: Safrica has no objection to Iran storing oil.
newsitem.headline: Safrica has no objection to Iran storing oil.

text.p: South African energy minister Penuell Maduna said Tuesday he had no objection to Iran using the Saldanha storage facility but that he was still waiting to see an environmental report on the issue.
Speaking at a conference in Edinburgh, Maduna also said there were two other bidders for space at the Strategic Fuel Fund's (SFF) oil storage terminal but he would not name them.
"The decision I have to make is based on the environmental study results which I am now told is on its way to my desk," Maduna said.

"It wouldn't matter so much who takes the space as long as they are going to pay a competitive rent to us. We want to maximise the profitablity of the space because space is becoming available as we are reducing to the internationally accepted level our crude reserves," he added.
"If Iran wants to bid against the others and wants to offer rent, I see no reason why we should not contract with Iran," Maduna said.
But he said Iran had told South African officials recently that it did not have crude to store right now.

The environmental study is being undertaken by the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research and was started at the beginning of 1996 after SFF had announced that Iran was interested in storing some of its surplus oil stocks at the 45 million barrel facility.
There was widespread public concern that the increased tanker traffic would have adverse environmental effects on the sensitive wetlands around Saldanha.
South Africa is in the process of reducing its oil stockpile built up under apartheid era sanctions.
The government decided last year to reduce the stockpile to 36 million barrels from 48 million barrels.
Maduna also said both Malaysia and Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest crude oil exporter, had indicated a "keen interest" in a fifth refinery in South Africa but he gave no further details.

He said Pretoria was keen to encourage vibrant competition in the energy sector, which should be open for both upstream and downstream projects. "Joint ventures of all sorts should be possible," he said.
